Article Title: Microsoft is hiring a legal engineer to teach lawyers across the company how to…
Article Text:
Microsoft wants a lawyer who can build AI agents, and it is paying up to $278,900 for one

Why Microsoft wants a lawyer who can also write software

The legal engineer job is spreading from startups to Big Tech

Microsoft has spent the past two years telling everyone else that AI is about to change how work gets done. Now it wants someone to prove the point inside its own legal department. The company has posted a job for a principal legal engineer, an unusual hybrid role that asks for a practising attorney who can also ship software, with base pay topping out at $278,900 a year.The listing, spotted on LinkedIn this week by Business Insider, puts the hire inside Microsoft's Customer & Partner Solutions group, the arm that supports the company's commercial business. The work is deliberately hands-on: building AI agents, sharpening prompts, and training attorneys and paralegals to actually use the tools. "This is a role for a builder," Microsoft wrote in the job description, adding that the person will partner directly with engineering rather than advise from the sidelines. Microsoft did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment.Lawyers were the corporate world's great tech holdouts for decades, understandably nervous about tools that could get one detail wrong in a 90-page agreement. That resistance is thinning. Clients are now pushing outside firms toward tools like Harvey and Claude for Legal to turn work around faster and bill less for it.The same pressure has moved in-house. Legal teams are betting that software can handle contract edits and policy drafting, letting them keep more of the early work and hand outside counsel matters that are already halfway done.Microsoft has a head start here because it builds some of these tools itself. Its lawyers already use Copilot for routine work, including contract review, where it compares a draft against similar agreements, flags issues and suggests edits that match company policy. Harvey is being rolled out across Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs.Until recently, legal engineer was mostly a startup title, filled by ex-lawyers with technical chops who sat close to customers. Palantir posted its own embedded legal engineer role last month, promising to turn manual workflows into automated ones.Microsoft wants a law degree and at least seven years of practice. Experience with Harvey or Copilot is preferred. Base pay starts at $147,000.
Article Summary: Microsoft has posted a job for a principal legal engineer, an unusual hybrid role. It asks for a practising attorney who can also ship software, with base pay topping out at $278,900. The work is deliberately hands-on: building AI agents, sharpening prompts, and training attorneys.

Article Title: America’s top VC Chamath Palihapitiya may have just told Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: You have failed miserably; lists three ‘biggest mistakes’
Article Text:
Political fallout in the Ohio Senate race

Chamath Palihapitiya points to three things that are needed

Chamath Palihapitiya, a prominent venture capitalist and “All-In Podcast” co-host, has issued a warning to the leaders of top artificial intelligence (AI) labs, arguing that the technology sector is currently sitting on a dangerous ‘powder keg’ caused by mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. According to Palihapitiya, the executive leadership leading cutting-edge AI development has failed to persuade citizens of the sector's merits and the community-level value of hosting infrastructure facilities.“Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy,” Palihapitiya said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).Palihapitiya’s remarks came as a direct reaction to reporting from Axios revealing that the campaign branch for Senate Republicans sent a stern memo to prominent AI development organizations. The communication from the National Republican Senatorial Committee pointed out that data centres have turned into a fierce campaign vulnerability in Ohio, where former Senator Sherrod Brown is competing in a tight race against Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted.Husted is running to complete the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term.“Texas, Pennsylvania and now Ohio. This is a powder keg and has the potential to unwind 200-300 basis points of annual GDP if it metastasizes. How did it get this bad? The collective leadership of frontier AI has failed miserably in doing the basics,” he added.The committee noted that the two candidates are locked in a dead heat, warning that data centers represent the heaviest anchor dragging down Husted's campaign.To repair the widening trust deficit, Palihapitiya advised industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message rather than relying on technical jargon or stoking doomsday scenarios.1. Paint a positive picture of what is possible with AI. Instead of spilling the ink on the glass half full, stories abound of pearl clutching, catastrophizing or arcane technical jargon that, together, breed mistrust, fear and skepticism.2. Visibly and disproportionately enrich the local communities AI data centers operate in. Tell these stories with a megaphone and have local leaders lead with the financial proof so it’s irrefutable.3. Stop infighting and stop trying to influence the government or trick them because of the asymmetric knowledge the industry has relative to outsiders and observers. This further makes it seem like a shady money grab to many bystanders.He stressed that companies must clearly demonstrate the positive everyday possibilities enabled by AI.
Article Summary: Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya says AI sector is sitting on a dangerous 'powder keg' He points to mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. He advises industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message.

Article Title: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna on his letter that ‘shocked’ business world, sent company's stock over 25 percent down, making it 'worst day' in IBM history
Article Text:
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna

Why IBM CEO thinks it was important to ‘tell’ beforehand

Facing an impending quarterly earnings miss driven by shifting enterprise IT budgets and rising AI distractions, IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna opted for radical transparency -- a move that triggered a historic stock plunge but is reported to have aligned with his core leadership philosophy. In an interview with CRN, IBM CEO Krishna detailed the high-stakes decision to pre-announce the 115-year-old tech giant's financial shortfall eight days before its scheduled July 22 earnings call. The disclosure sent IBM shares tumbling more than 25%, marking one of the steepest single-day declines in the company's history.IBM's underperformance stemmed from enterprise clients pausing infrastructure projects to front-load spending on data center hardware amid supply constraints and surging costs. Additionally, Krishna noted that customer attention had been diverted by security debates surrounding an AI model released by Anthropic. He reduced IBM's expected full-year revenue growth for the year by more than $600 million, saying that the fall is in part due to some clients pushing out IBM infrastructure projects to pay for the growing cost of supply constrained memory, storage, servers and other data center infrastructure.Rather than holding the bad news for the standard earnings cycle, Krishna fell back on a long-standing operating principle: "If there’s a hard thing to be done, do it earlier rather than later," Krishna told CRN.By clearing the bad news early, Krishna aimed to pivot the official earnings call away from post-mortem explanations and toward strategic fixes. "Time will tell whether that was the right decision. I tend to think it was," Krishna said. "Otherwise, we would have been spending the last week explaining the hesitation as opposed to what we are going to do to go fix it."The decision highlights the pressures facing IBM as it balances heavy investments in generative AI and long-term quantum computing against Wall Street's short-term expectations. When asked by CRN about potential vulnerability to activist investors or board friction following the market reaction, the CEO, who took the helm in April 2020, remained pragmatic about corporate oversight."If you falter, one should always be just prepared is my view," Krishna said, adding that public CEOs must constantly evaluate whether they are delivering sufficient returns. "And activists, at the end, if I look at the good side, are trying to come in to say, 'I need better returns for clients and for investors.' And if that’s the goal, then one should be prepared to deal with them. That is just the nature of today’s world that we live in. "Krishna maintained that his primary strategy to protect the company's innovation roadmap remains centered on client satisfaction and workforce investment.IBM CEO Krishna reasoned the Q2 weakness to deal ‘deferral, and not destruction’. He said, “This was deferral and not destruction.” Krishna made the statement while talking to analysts during IBM’s latest quarterly earnings call with analysts. Krishna’s confidence comes in part from the fact that one-third of those largest infrastructure projects requiring a lot of customer CapEx have already closed.
Article Summary: IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna opted for radical transparency. The disclosure sent IBM shares tumbling more than 25%, marking one of the steepest single-day declines in the company's history. Krishna: "If there’s a hard thing to be done, do it earlier rather than later"

Article Title: Deep Talent Technologies launches EZ Refer, an AI-powered referral platform
Article Text: DeepTalent Technologies has launched Ezrefer, a platform that lets any professional refer someone from their network to an open role, track that referral through to hire, and get paid automatically when the candidate joins. It is live now at ezrefer.ai, open to professionals and employers across India.“Referrals already produce some of the best hires companies make. Twenty years in recruitment has shown me that. Companies already believe it enough to pay for it, but only while you’re on their payroll. The moment you leave, or if you were never employed there at all, there is no financial reward, even when the referral leads to the most senior hire. India has one of the largest pools of skilled professionals anywhere in the world, and most of it sits outside every company’s referral scheme. Ezrefer is the infrastructure that closes that gap: referral hiring built as a real workflow, open to any professional’s network,” said Richa Bajaj, Founder, DeepTalent Technologies.Among the first recruiting firms on the platform is The Glove, a 21-year-old executive search firm bringing a network built across BFSI, aerospace, engineering, ITES, industrial automation, automobile and e-commerce.
Article Summary: DeepTalent Technologies has launched Ezrefer, a platform that lets any professional refer someone from their network to an open role. It is live now at ezrefer.ai, open to professionals and employers across India. Among the first recruiting firms on the platform is The Glove, a 21-year-old executive search firm.

Article Title: In 2023, Canadian wildfires cut solar power generation by 6.38 TWh across North America and Europe, causing an estimated $1.9 billion loss
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Canadian wildfire smoke affected solar power generation

Other factors affecting solar power generation

Wildfires can also damage solar panels and equipment

Wildfires may be adversely affecting solar power generation worldwide. According to a recent study published in Nature, smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours (TWh) over five months. The researchers estimated that the reduction amounted to about 2.8% of the solar electricity generated across the two regions during that period.The report also estimated that the decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires that blocked or scattered sunlight before it could reach solar panels, though they noted significant uncertainty around the estimates.The 2023 Canadian wildfire season produced large amounts of smoke that travelled across North America and reached parts of Europe. The researchers modelled the atmospheric effects of the wildfire emissions over five months to estimate their impact on solar electricity generation.Sunlight is absorbed and scattered by particles in the atmosphere. This results in less sunlight reaching the solar panels, and installations producing less electricity even if the panels themselves are not directly affected by fire.The findings also show how the effects of wildfires can extend beyond areas immediately surrounding the fires. Solar farms, commercial installations and rooftop systems can all be affected when smoke moves through the atmosphere above them.Wildfire smoke is not the only source of air pollution that decreases the productivity of solar panel arrays. Pollution particles (particulate matter) released into the air by automobiles and coal-burning electrical generators may decrease how much sunlight enters your solar array.Dust can affect panels in different ways by settling directly on the panel surface . Dust accumulation from construction and mining activities can reduce electricity generation if panels are not cleaned.Improved solar-power forecasting can help grid operators prepare for generation changes caused by smoke. More accurate forecasts can help operators anticipate declines in solar output and arrange alternative electricity sources to maintain the balance between supply and demand.According to Cornell University, researchers studied a machine learning model for predicting solar energy production during certain extreme wildfire smoke OPS events in 2025. Researchers indicated that the model has more detail and accuracy than the New York grid operator's forecasts.Emissions from automobiles and factories are a source of atmospheric pollution. These can be reduced with improved dust management at solar farms. This will limit the effects of pollution on the farms’ ability to generate electricity.Wildfire smoke can affect solar generation without physically damaging an installation, but fires can also directly threaten solar farms. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified wildfire damage as a risk to photovoltaic systems, including potential damage to panels and components used to operate them.A solar farm owned by a French company Luxel was affected by a wildfire last month. The fire broke out in southern France in July 2026. About 100 of the 43,500 panels and some cables were damaged in the blaze, while the transformers and inverters were not harmed.Vegetation management around the site helped limit the fire's reach. Luxel said that regular clearing work, including a 50-meter perimeter around the fences, helped prevent flames from reaching most of the installation.The US Department of Energy recommends maintaining defensible space around solar installations in areas exposed to wildfire risk. Its measures include managing vegetation, paving areas around critical equipment, placing important electrical components in fire-resistant containers, maintaining access for firefighters and keeping an updated wildfire emergency-response plan.The Canadian wildfire study illustrates how fires can affect solar power production without reaching a solar energy facility, and physical damage to infrastructure is an additional risk to facilities built in wildland-urban interface areas.
Article Summary: Smoke from the Canadian wildfires in 2023 reduced solar electricity generation across North America and Europe by an estimated 6.38 terawatt-hours. The decline in solar generation caused an economic loss of about $1.9 billion and was associated with about 2.1 megatons of CO2 emissions. Researchers attributed the drop to smoke and airborne particles from the wildfires.

Article Title: Gates Foundation makes landmark 10-year donation of $540 million to University of Washington with the aim to support ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

"Reliable and independent evidence can mean the difference between reacting to a health crisis after it has taken hold and acting early enough to change its course,"

Gates Foundation grant will expand Global Burden of Disease study

University of Washington and Gates Foundation expand health research partnership

"Every government and funder faces difficult decisions about where to invest limited resources for greatest impact, and those decisions depend on trusted evidence,"

"For nearly two decades, IHME has been one of the foundation’s most important global partners, helping us, governments, researchers, and global health partners around the world understand where health is improving, where progress is stalling, and where action is needed most. Our long-term commitment recognises the value of this work to strengthen a shared evidence base that will continue to inform decisions to improve—and save—millions of lives.

"

IHME to provide more local health evidence

"Reliable and independent evidence can mean the difference between reacting to a health crisis after it has taken hold and acting early enough to change its course,"

"This investment will allow us to provide high-quality evidence at a much more local level and help leaders understand not only where health is improving or worsening, but which decisions can make the greatest difference for people."

"The Gates Foundation has been a steadfast partner of the University of Washington for decades, and we are grateful for its generous support. The UW is committed to improving the health of people in Washington and around the world, and this investment will expand IHME’s already significant impact, which will mean longer, healthier lives for countless people," s

"We are deeply grateful to the Gates Foundation for this extraordinary investment in IHME and the University of Washington School of Medicine,"

"Their longstanding partnership has helped make it possible for IHME to deliver trusted health evidence around the world. This new grant will extend that impact by giving leaders data that are comprehensive and comparable to guide decisions that help improve the health of communities and save lives."

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates’ the Gates Foundation have awarded a major donation to the University of Washington's Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME). The $540.2 million, 10-year grant will help the health institute expand the availability and geographic detail of health data used by governments, researchers and health professionals. The investment will support the expansion of the Global Burden of Disease study, along with IHME's health forecasting and global health-spending research.The grant is the largest charitable grant ever given to the University of Washington and will expand the Global Burden of Disease study from about 925 locations to nearly 5,000.said Dr Christopher J.L. Murray, IHME director and professor of health metrics sciences.The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study is a large-scale assessment of health trends and conditions across countries. Under the new grant, IHME will expand the number of locations covered by the study, providing more detailed local-level information.The 10-year funding will also support IHME's work on health forecasting and future scenarios, as well as its tracking of health spending worldwide. Together, these areas are intended to provide information on current health conditions, potential future changes and how health resources are being used.Murray, who is the grant's principal investigator, began the GBD study in the early 1990s and has led its development through a research network that now includes more than 20,000 collaborators across more than 150 countries and territories.The Gates Foundation and the state of Washington provided the founding investment that established IHME at the University of Washington in 2007. The institute operates as an independent research organisation within the UW School of Medicine and makes its research and findings freely available to countries, researchers and communities.The new grant builds on the foundation's longstanding support for IHME and its work in health measurement. The institute has developed methods and standards used in health metrics research and has worked with researchers and institutions worldwide to expand the use of health data.said Mark Suzman, Chief Executive Officer of the Gates Foundation.The expanded research comes as countries face multiple health threats alongside pressure on public and global health budgets. IHME's work under the new grant will focus on producing more detailed, timely evidence to help governments and health organisations identify health needs and assess possible future scenarios.Murray said.The University of Washington said the investment will expand IHME's existing research activities and its ability to provide health evidence in Washington, across the United States and internationally.aid UW President Robert J. Jones.Timothy Dellit, CEO of UW Medicine and dean of the University of Washington School of Medicine, said the grant would support IHME's continued work providing health evidence to decision-makers.said Dellit, CEO of UW Medicine and dean of the University of Washington School of Medicine.The grant will provide IHME with 10 years of funding for the expanded GBD study, health forecasting and health-spending research, while its findings will remain freely available to users regardless of their income or access to commercial data systems.
Article Summary: Gates Foundation grant will expand Global Burden of Disease study. 10-year funding will also support IHME's work on health forecasting and future scenarios, as well as its tracking of health spending worldwide. Grant is the largest charitable grant ever given to the University of Washington.

Article Title: Australia passes law to tax Google, Meta and Microsoft if they do not pay for local news
Article Text:
Funding local media and journalism in Australia

Rules for tax offsets and content agreements

Australia has formally enacted new legislation that requires major technology corporations to pay substantial levies if they do not negotiate commercial compensation agreements with domestic news publishers for distributing their journalism. According to a report by news agency Reuters, the law is titled News Bargaining Incentive, and imposes a 2.5% tax on local advertising earnings unless qualifying platforms enter into direct content partnerships with Australian media organisations.Funds generated from the tax will be channeled directly to domestic Australian newsrooms, the report said, adding that lawmakers highlighted that local journalistic reporting plays a major role in keeping users engaged and generating digital ad income across large tech platforms.The regulation specifically covers digital platforms operating major search or social networks in Australia that generate more than A$250 million (roughly $178 million) in domestic advertising revenue. Key companies subject to the framework include Google-parent Alphabet, Facebook-parent company Meta, Microsoft-owned LinkedIn and TikTok.Big Tech platforms can bypass the 2.5% tax by entering into commercial agreements with a minimum of eight distinct news publishers before their financial reporting cycle concludes.The financial value of these partnerships will reduce their total tax obligation. Under the guidelines, commercial agreements must directly fund the creation of news reporting or address how a publisher's digital reporting is hosted and shared on the platform.The legislation also says that financial investments made with major media organisations provide a 150% tax deduction credit, while agreements signed with small and mid-sized publishers grant a 200% offset credit. No individual publisher agreement can account for more than 25% of a platform's total levy obligation.“The ⁠legislation is here, and the message to platforms to pursue commercial deals is clear. Deals will need ​to be finalised before the end of a ​digital platform's ⁠financial reporting period to be used to offset their liability in that period. This is an important day ⁠for ​Australian news businesses and Australian journalism,” the government said.The approval of the News Bargaining Incentive follows closely behind another major legislative measure passed a day earlier, which placed broad curbs on gambling advertising.
Article Summary: New law imposes a 2.5% tax on local advertising earnings unless qualifying platforms enter into direct content partnerships with Australian media organisations. Key companies subject to the framework include Google-parent Alphabet, Facebook-parent company Meta, Microsoft-owned LinkedIn and TikTok.

Article Title: Former employee claims that Meta had a ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’ policy on child safety issues
Article Text:
Former Meta employee accuses company of ignoring risks

Meta rejects allegations

Poll Vote & Share your view How serious do you think the mental health crisis among teens linked to social media is? Very serious Somewhat serious Not serious at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Former Meta safety researcher Arturo Béjar has accused the company of ignoring child safety concerns to protect its business, telling a California federal court that Meta had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” policy when it came to underage users. Arturo Béjar made the claims while testifying in a major trial brought by 29 US states, which accuse Meta of harming children and teenagers through Facebook and Instagram. He also criticised Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg , saying the executive did not do enough to address safety concerns despite having broad control over the company.Arturo Béjar worked on Meta's safety team from 2009 to 2015 and later returned as a consultant between 2019 and 2021. He told jurors that he had raised safety issues with Zuckerberg at least 100 times.“You just cannot trust Mark Zuckerberg with kids,” Béjar said during his testimony. He also accused Zuckerberg of creating a misleading impression about Meta's commitment to protecting young users.“I felt that he created a false and misleading impression of Facebook’s commitment to young people,” Béjar said.According to Béjar, Meta had the ability to identify children who were getting around age-related safety measures but chose not to act aggressively.He said the company had a “don’t ask, don’t tell” approach because of concerns about its business. “Where the youngest kids are is where the users are going to be in the future,” Béjar said.The trial, started on August 18 is expected to last about six weeks. Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify. The 29 states accuse Meta of contributing to a teen mental health crisis through the design of its platforms. They are also seeking changes to Facebook and Instagram and major financial penalties.Lawyers for the states have said the damages could approach $200 billion, while Meta has argued that the potential exposure could reach $1.4 trillion.Meta has denied wrongdoing. During opening arguments, Meta lawyer Paul Schmidt said Zuckerberg and other company leaders had taken steps to protect children online, including parental controls and time limits for social media use.
Article Summary: Arturo Béjar worked on Meta's safety team from 2009 to 2015 and later returned as a consultant between 2019 and 2021. He told jurors that he had raised safety issues with Zuckerberg at least 100 times. 29 states accuse Meta of contributing to a teen mental health crisis through the design of its platforms.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says AI boom is driving up smartphone, laptop prices; warns ‘Sticker shock’ may get worse
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu compares AI boom with telecom bubble

Here’s what Sridhar Vembu wrote on X

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu recently shared an X post warning that massive spending on AI is pushing up costs across the technology supply chain, from memory chips and CPUs to GPUs, power systems and cooling equipment. Sridhar Vembu believes the AI technology itself will eventually reach its full potential, but says the investment boom behind it could end like the telecom bubble of the late 1990s. In the post, Vembu pointed to the higher prices consumers are seeing when upgrading their smartphones and laptops in 2026. “The sticker shock seen by anyone trying to upgrade their smart phone or laptop in 2026?” he wrote on X.Vembu linked the price pressure to the huge amount of money being invested in AI infrastructure. According to Vembu, the boom has affected markets ranging from electric power generation and transformers to diesel backup generators, cooling systems, memory, CPUs and GPUs.Sridhar Vembu said the fact that a technology is real does not mean the investment boom around it cannot become a bubble. He compared today's AI boom with the telecom investment boom between 1995 and 2000. High-speed optical fibre, which was one of the technologies behind that investment cycle, eventually became widely available, including in remote areas.“It is important to keep in mind that the technology can be real and become ubiquitous (like how high speed optical fiber connections are now available in remote villages like mine, the premise behind the telecom investment bubble of 1995-2000). Yet that did not prevent most telecom equipment companies from going bankrupt in 2001-3,” he said in the post.“The AI credit boom will meet the same fate, and I actually do believe the technology will achieve its full potential,” Vembu said."The sticker shock seen by anyone trying to upgrade their smart phone or laptop in 2026?That is the AI investment boom, funded (ultimately) by the mother of all credit bubbles unleashed post pandemic. It has distorted markets ranging from electric power generation, transformers, diesel back up generators, cooling systems, memory, CPUs and of course, GPUs.It is important to keep in mind that the technology can be real and become ubiquitous (like how high speed optical fiber connections are now available in remote villages like mine, the premise behind the telecom investment bubble of 1995-2000). Yet that did not prevent most telecom equipment companies from going bankrupt in 2001-3.The AI credit boom will meet the same fate, and I actually do believe the technology will achieve its full potential.Staying positive on the tech while being careful to not lose one's shirt in the bubble unleashed by boosters of the same tech - that is the careful balancing act needed today."
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu recently shared an X post warning that massive spending on AI is pushing up costs across the technology supply chain. He compared today's AI boom with the telecom investment boom between 1995 and 2000. “The AI credit boom will meet the same fate, and I actually do believe the technology will achieve its full potential,” he said.

Article Title: Startup founded by three Harvard dropouts that tech investors warned of saying 'don’t back kids in chips' is pulling talent from Nvidia; engineer says ...
Article Text:
Etched co-founders Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu. (Image source: WSJ)

Investors once warned ‘Don’t back the kids in chips’

Etched is hiring from Nvidia

A chip startup once viewed by investors as too inexperienced to take on the semiconductor industry is now pulling engineers from Nvidia and other major chip companies, as it moves closer to becoming a serious player in AI hardware. Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative-trading firm Jane Street as its first customer, booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. The hiring trend has also surprised some of its new employees. Former Nvidia systems engineer Anthony Gamerman said he kept hearing about colleagues leaving Nvidia for Etched. “One leaves, and then another one, you hear a couple weeks later, and you go, ‘Whoa, I can’t believe so-and-so is heading over to Etched,’” he said.Etched was started by Robert Wachen, Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu, who are all 24 years old. The company initially struggled to attract investors because of the founders' limited experience in semiconductor hardware.Sonya Huang, a general partner at Sequoia Capital, described the concern among investors at the time. “Among tech investors, the prevailing wisdom was ‘don’t back the kids in chips,’” Huang said.She added that investors believed young founders could succeed in internet businesses but faced much bigger challenges when building semiconductor hardware.Etched has since raised nearly $2 billion, including a new $700 million funding round led by Jane Street that values the company at $21 billion.The startup has built a team with significant semiconductor experience. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia, according to Etched. The company has also hired engineers from other established semiconductor firms.Brian Loiler, who spent nearly 23 years at Nvidia, joined Etched to work on its servers and racks. He has since helped recruit about a dozen Nvidia engineers to the startup, with some turning down counteroffers. Jimmy Daley, a former Nvidia vice president of data-center systems engineering who retired in July, is also an investor in Etched.The company has developed AI processors designed specifically for this workload. Its first customer is Jane Street, a quantitative trading firm that uses powerful computing systems to run trading models quickly. Etched says it has already started shipping its chips and took just 44 days to get its test chips running inference workloads after receiving them from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.“We may be the only AI chip that was built by a startup that was successful on the first try,” Etched co-founder and president Robert Wachen said.
Article Summary: Etched, founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, has signed quantitative- trading firm Jane Street as its first customer. The company has booked more than $1 billion in orders and started shipping its AI chips. Around 15% of its roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Peter Theil, ‘You should focus relentlessly on something you’re good at doing, but before that you must think hard about whether it will be valuable in the future’
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Peter Thiel

What Peter Thiel's quote means

Why this runs against popular advice

Applying the idea beyond startups

A simple takeaway

Peter Thiel co-founded PayPal , was the first outside investor in Facebook, and went on to build Palantir Technologies and the venture capital firm Founders Fund, establishing himself as one of Silicon Valley's most influential, and most contrarian, thinkers. In his 2014 book Zero to One, co-authored with Blake Masters, Thiel lays out a set of ideas about how to build lasting value in business and career, several of which directly challenge conventional wisdom about hard work, passion and talent. This quote is one of the clearest examples of that contrarian streak."You should focus relentlessly on something you're good at doing, but before that you must think hard about whether it will be valuable in the future."The quote directly challenges a piece of advice repeated constantly in schools, universities and career guidance: that it doesn't really matter what you choose to do, as long as you do it well. Thiel argues this is simply false. In his view, competence alone doesn't guarantee value, because being excellent at something the world doesn't need, or no longer needs, still leaves a person without real leverage or reward.The quote sets up a specific order of operations. Most advice about success emphasizes effort and mastery first: work hard, get good at something, and the rewards will follow. Thiel flips the sequence. Before investing years into becoming excellent at a skill, he argues, the more important question is whether that skill will actually hold value once that mastery is achieved. Skill built on a shrinking or already-saturated foundation, no matter how impressive, has a much lower ceiling than skill built on a genuinely growing one.This idea sits in tension with the popular "follow your passion" narrative, which treats enthusiasm and effort as the main ingredients of a fulfilling and successful career. Thiel isn't dismissing passion or hard work; he's arguing they're necessary but insufficient. Effort applied to the wrong target can produce extraordinary skill that the market simply doesn't reward, an outcome that can be more discouraging than falling short of a lesser goal, precisely because the effort was real and the payoff still didn't materialize.In Zero to One, Thiel extends this logic even to entrepreneurship itself, cautioning that even highly talented people shouldn't necessarily start their own company just because they could. Someone who deeply understands how disproportionately outcomes can vary between ventures, a concept he refers to as the power law, might do better joining an already fast-growing company than founding a new one from scratch, since the differences between companies tend to dwarf the differences between roles within them.The quote's core lesson extends well past the startup world. Choosing what to study, which industry to enter, or which skill to spend years developing all carry the same underlying risk: if the surrounding landscape shifts, mastery built on outdated assumptions can lose much of its value, regardless of how much effort went into acquiring it. This doesn't mean chasing every emerging trend either; it means treating the question of future relevance as seriously as the question of personal aptitude, rather than assuming skill alone will always find its market.Thiel's quote works as a corrective to the idea that hard work and mastery are automatically rewarded. Talent and effort matter, but they only compound in value when aimed at something the future actually needs. The more useful question isn't simply "what am I good at," but "will being good at this still matter," a distinction that can be the difference between mastery that pays off and mastery that simply goes unnoticed.
Article Summary: Peter Thiel co-founded PayPal and was the first outside investor in Facebook. In his 2014 book Zero to One, Thiel lays out a set of ideas about how to build lasting value in business and career. Thiel argues competence alone doesn't guarantee value, because being excellent at something the world doesn't need, still leaves a person without real leverage or reward.

Article Title: 82% of Indians now want AI in their phone, but battery is still the deal-breaker: Amazon survey
Article Text:
FILE - This Sept. 6, 2012, file photo, shows the Amazon logo. (AP Photo/Reed Saxon, File)

What Indian buyers actually want from smartphone AI

Smartphone budgets are climbing, and reviews beat discounts

AI has stopped being a selling point and become a checkbox. Amazon.in's first Best in Tech Survey, run in July 2026 with more than 40,000 responses, found that AI features now shape the purchase decision for 82% of smartphone buyers in India. What buyers actually want from it, though, is narrower than most launch keynotes suggest.The fundamentals have not moved an inch. Performance and speed influenced 87% of respondents, battery life 79% and camera quality 77%. Battery is also where phones are failing hardest: 22% named it as the one thing their current phone must fix, ahead of camera at 17% and performance at 12%.Contextual assistance topped the AI wishlist at 25%, meaning features that read what is on screen and offer something useful without being asked. Generative photo editing followed at 18%, visual search at 17% and adaptive battery management at 11%. That last one is telling. Even the AI feature buyers want is mostly about surviving the day."How customers buy a smartphone today has changed," said Zeba Khan, Director, Consumer Electronics, Amazon India, adding that Amazon built the survey because most claims about Indian buyers are inferred rather than asked.The Rs 25,000 to Rs 50,000 band remains the biggest at 42%, but one in three buyers is now considering Rs 50,000 or more, including 17% shopping above Rs 75,000. That premium appetite is not a metro story either: Tier-3 cities accounted for 15% of it against 18% for metros.Buyers are also doing homework. Reviews and ratings mattered to 47% at the point of decision, against 35% for price and deals. More than half hold on to a phone for two years, yet 48% plan to upgrade within three months.
Article Summary: Amazon.in's first Best in Tech Survey, run in July 2026 with more than 40,000 responses, found that AI features now shape the purchase decision for 82% of smartphone buyers in India. What buyers actually want from it, though, is narrower than most launch keynotes suggest.

Article Title: Walmart employees working at retailer's stores have a new responsibility that they are very unhappy about: Correcting ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Walmart employees are dealing with AI-assigned tasks and errors

Walmart AI safety alerts create another issue for workers

Walmart employees are reportedly taking on a new responsibility. As the retailer expands its use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in stores, the company may have asked its store staff to correct and clean up AI mistakes. The company is reportedly rolling out AI assistants that assign tasks and monitor store employees through the MyWalmart app. However, workers have claimed that the AI systems can sometimes miss the context needed to reflect how work is actually done in the stores.The AI rollout has also raised concerns about inaccurate task times, irrelevant safety alerts, and performance expectations. A store-level HR manager told Business Insider that an AI task-assigning agent “just assumes that they're going to be perfect every single time.” However, Walmart says employee feedback is essential to improving the tools and that workers are not punished for failing to follow technology guidance.Workers at stores where the AI features have launched can receive tasks and targets through the MyWalmart app on company-provided phones. The system is intended to help associates plan their shifts and can learn from patterns in their work.Elizabeth Nigh, an asset protection manager in Wisconsin, told Business Insider that AI-generated task lists can help associates who otherwise have to wait for a manager to assign work.She said the system can learn where an employee works most effectively and reflect that in future assignments.Other workers said the technology does not always account for the steps involved in completing a task. Restocking shelves, for example, can require checking expiration dates, removing damaged products and cleaning dust or spills in addition to putting merchandise on shelves.The HR manager said her store does not discipline employees when AI-generated performance metrics do not match what happens in practice. “We're not going to hold people to these impossible standards,” she said.An online fulfilment worker also told Business Insider that she has struggled to match the times projected by the AI app for picking general merchandise orders because its suggested routes can take workers through different parts of the store.The Walmart-owned Spark delivery service has also introduced a “smart path” feature that some drivers said can direct them to collect frozen products early in a shopping trip. One worker said this creates “extra time and energy I could be spending on the next order.”Walmart is also using an AI agent to monitor store safety through security cameras and sensors. The system can flag potential problems such as spills or refrigerators operating outside safe temperature ranges.Some workers said the system can generate alerts that require them to provide additional context or determine whether an issue actually needs attention. The online fulfilment worker said she receives numerous safety alerts through the Walmart app when using her personal phone to clock in and out.Her response to alerts she considers irrelevant is straightforward: “I ignore them.”Brooks Forrest, Walmart's vice president for associate tools, said stores have flexibility in how they use the technology. “We do not punish people for not following the tech guidance,” he said.Forrest also said his team regularly visits stores and holds listening sessions to understand how the tools perform in real-world settings. “The technology is there to help them, but they ultimately have the say in what they do,” he said.
Article Summary: Walmart is reportedly rolling out AI assistants that assign tasks and monitor store employees through the MyWalmart app. Workers have claimed that the AI systems can sometimes miss the context needed to reflect how work is actually done in the stores. The AI rollout has also raised concerns about inaccurate task times, irrelevant safety alerts, and performance expectations.

Article Title: Fujifilm X-Space in Delhi goes three floors: Cameras, instax and a first service centre
Article Text:
Fujifilm's Delhi X-Space is now a three-floor imaging hub with a service centre.

Fujifilm India has reopened its Delhi X-Space as a three-floor imaging destination, expanding the centre it first opened in the capital in 2023. The upgraded space now carries the company's full Imaging Solutions portfolio under one roof, from X Series and GFX System cameras and lenses to the instax range, Fujinon binoculars, QuickSnap film cameras and printing solutions.The bigger change is what sits above the shop floor. The second level holds a curated photo exhibition of images shot on Fujifilm cameras, alongside a working studio for live demonstrations and studio tests. That studio includes an editing set-up for film-grading and image-editing sessions, so visitors can actually see what the files look like after the shutter click rather than judging a camera by its grip.The third floor houses Fujifilm's first customer service centre in Delhi, which is arguably the most practical addition here. Owners have long had to route repairs and support through other channels, and putting service in the same building as the demo counter closes a gap that regional buyers notice more than marketing does.The first floor is the main experience centre, split into zones by category, with product demonstrations and workshops planned for visitors at different skill levels.Haruto Iwata, Managing Director, Fujifilm Asia Pacific, said India is an important market for the company, supported by a community of photography enthusiasts and professionals. Koji Wada, Managing Director, Fujifilm India, tied the expansion to the group's stated purpose of "giving our world more smiles" and creating closer engagement with its technologies.Arun Babu, Associate Director, Imaging Solutions Division, Fujifilm India, said the intent is for visitors to explore the breadth of the portfolio firsthand, across product experiences, studio tests, exhibitions and service.
Article Summary: Fujifilm India reopens its Delhi X-Space as a three-floor imaging destination. The first floor is the main experience centre, split into zones by category. The second level holds a curated photo exhibition and a working studio. The third floor houses the company's first customer service centre in Delhi.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Larry Page: ‘Lots of companies don't succeed over time’
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Google co-founder Larry Page

Breaking down what Larry Page actually meant

How Larry Page’s thinking shaped Google

Why this quote still holds up

Larry Page does not talk much these days. The Google co-founder now spends most of his time out of the public eye and has always been a man of few words when he does choose to speak. But when he does, people tend to listen closely, because his track record of predicting where technology is headed is hard to argue with. Page founded Google in a garage with a mission to provide people with the knowledge of the world on their computers and personal devices. He is one half of the Google founder with Sergey Brin being the second. Page also served as CEO of Google twice."Lots of companies don't succeed over time. What do they fundamentally do wrong? They usually miss the future."This particular quote sums up something Page has believed since the earliest days of Google, and it's a line worth sitting with for a while. At first glance, this sounds almost too simple to be useful advice. Of course companies that fail miss something. But look closer at the wording and you'll notice Page is talking about an entire shift in direction that a company failed to see coming, or saw coming and chose to ignore anyway.His second stint as the CEO focussed on core strategy before transitioning to lead Alphabet – a reorganised entity with Google becoming its largest subsidiary and the umbrella company for Internet interests.Page has repeated versions of this idea across interviews and internal talks at Google over the years. His argument has always been that most businesses collapse because leadership gets comfortable with what already works, and by the time the world has moved on, it's too late to catch up.There's also an interesting undertone here about ego. Missing the future, in Page's framing, isn't usually a technical failure but a mindset failure. Executives get attached to the products that made them successful in the first place, and that attachment blinds them to warning signs. Page has always tried to build Google, and later Alphabet, around the opposite instinct, which is to spend money on things that look uncertain today because uncertainty is often where the next big shift is hiding.Page’s idea is baked into how Google actually operates, or at least how it operated when Page was more hands-on. The company’s willingness to pour money into projects before others (or ahead of time) suggests this: self-driving cars, life sciences research, even early bets on AI long before it became the industry's obsession traces directly back to this philosophy. Page wanted Google to be the company doing the disrupting rather than the one getting disrupted.Alphabet’s restructuring in 2015, which separated Google's core business from its more experimental ventures, was itself an extension of this thinking. Page wanted room for ideas that wouldn't look profitable for years, maybe ever, because he believed that's exactly where the next Google-sized opportunity would eventually come from.Fast forward to today, and the tech industry is once again going through one of those moments Page warned about. AI is transforming the way software is being built, search for information, and run whole industries. Companies that bet their present advantage would last forever are now racing to catch up.
Article Summary: Google co-founder Larry Page has a track record of predicting where technology is headed. Page founded Google in a garage with a mission to provide people with the knowledge of the world on their computers and personal devices. He is one half of the Google founder with Sergey Brin being the second.

“Derek Chauvin was unjustly convicted of murder, therefore he should be freed. The facts show that he was not the cause of death, nor did he at any time intend for a death to occur. Whatever else he may be, he is not a murderer. That is the truth.”

Derek Chauvin asks court to pause current appeal

Derek Chauvin's previous conviction relief petition

George Floyd murder conviction

Derek Chauvin has requested to challenge his conviction in the murder of George Floyd. The former Minneapolis police officer has asked a Minnesota appeals court to pause his current appeal while he pursues new claims about how his case was prosecuted. Tesla CEO Elon Musk has also supported Chauvin’s bid to overturn the conviction.In a post shared on the microblogging site X (formerly Twitter), Musk wrote,Chauvin’s attorneys are seeking to send the case back to the trial court to raise claims including that Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz unlawfully assigned Attorney General Keith Ellison to prosecute the case.According to a report by the New York Post, Chauvin’s attorneys filed the latest motion this week, asking the Minnesota Court of Appeals to stay his pending appeal. The request would allow his case to return to the local trial court so his defence can present a new claim that his original charges were unlawfully brought.According to the motion, Chauvin’s legal team argues that Minnesota Gov.Tim Walz unlawfully assigned Attorney General Keith Ellison to prosecute the case. The filing describes this and other alleged procedural violations as “structural errors” that, according to the defence, cannot be waived.The claims include improper prosecutor assignment, failure to convene a grand jury, lack of court jurisdiction and judicial bias.The latest filing is Chauvin’s third petition seeking post-conviction relief. His defence previously appealed a judge’s decision denying an earlier petition.The judge rejected Chauvin’s entire post-conviction petition on May 1, more than five months after it was filed in November 2025. Chauvin’s legal team then filed an appeal in June challenging that decision.The current motion seeks to pause that appeal while the trial court considers the newly raised procedural claims.Chauvin was convicted in April 2021 in connection with Floyd’s death in 2020. Records cited in the case state that Chauvin knelt on Floyd’s neck for nine minutes and 29 seconds while Floyd was face down and handcuffed on the ground.Floyd suffered a fatal lack of oxygen to the brain, according to the records provided. Chauvin’s conviction and subsequent efforts to obtain post-conviction relief have continued through multiple court filings.Musk’s comments on X came as Chauvin’s attorneys sought to have the latest procedural claims considered by the state court system. Article Title: Anthropic says Claude designed protein binders for 14 of 15 test targets, with independent labs validating hundreds of designs; an early sign of how AI could speed parts of biological research
Article Text:
Claude designed protein binders against 14 of 15 targets, with independent labs confirming 354 hits

How Claude ran a protein design campaign with almost no human input

Where Claude beat published benchmarks, and where it flatly failed

Claude Opus 5 matched a contract lab's purity reading in under 20 minutes

Anthropic says its Claude models designed working protein binders against 14 of 15 targets in a campaign that outside labs then physically built and tested, a result the company is framing as early proof that AI can absorb parts of biological research that normally eat months of a specialist's time. The designs came out of sessions where Claude was left largely alone after the opening prompt, then handed to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience for validation.The numbers do most of the arguing. Claude produced 354 confirmed binders out of 1,320 designs. Hit rates came in at 26.7% for Mythos Preview and 22.6% for Opus 4.8 when the models attacked all targets at once, rising to 35.1% when Mythos Preview worked one target at a time. Anthropic pegs the current field average at 10% to 15%.A binder, or minibinder, is a small protein built to latch onto a target protein, which is roughly how a large share of modern medicine works. Designing one from scratch has historically meant weeks of computation and screening.Claude got 48 hours of wall time, up to 12,500 NVIDIA H100 hours, a roughly 30,000-token prompt, internet access, and connectors for Google Drive, Slack, Gmail and BioRxiv.From there it picked where on each target to bind, orchestrated existing open-source design and folding models, ran optimisation cycles, and screened candidates. Human involvement came down to approving access requests, watching the infrastructure, and ordering the winning designs.Against RBX1, Mythos Preview hit 40% in single-target mode, against 3.7% for human entrants in Adaptyv Bio's competition. Its best design outperformed the contest winner, which had come out of 245 entries.TNFα produced the odder result. Opus 4.8 designed binders that worked across human, cynomolgus monkey and mouse versions of the protein, which matters for animal testing. Mythos Preview, the more capable model, failed on it entirely. Anthropic admits it does not know why.Maltose-binding protein was a clean loss. None of the 90 designs bound. BBF-14, a synthetic beta-barrel used precisely because it is novel, yielded three binders with modest affinity.The second experiment used the publicly available Opus 5 on analytical chemistry. Given raw NMR and LC-MS files from a contract lab and a two-sentence prompt, with no vendor software, Claude returned finished results in 23 and 19 minutes. It measured purity at 96.4% against the lab's 96.33%, and matched hydrogen counts within 0.08. The LC-MS file used an undocumented proprietary format, so Claude reverse-engineered the encoding and verified it by reproducing the instrument's own totals across 2,664 scans. The lab's own report arrived four days after the first spectrum.Anthropic acknowledges the dual-use risk here. Protein design remains blocked in Fable 5, its most capable generally available model, with a scientist access programme promised soon.
Article Summary: Claude models designed protein binders against 14 of 15 targets. Independent labs confirmed 354 hits out of 1,320 designs. Hit rates came in at 26.7% for Mythos Preview and 22.6% for Opus 4.8. Human involvement came down to approving access requests.

Article Title: App of the Week: ProShot turns your phone into a full-blown DSLR camera
Article Text:
Available on: Android, iOS

Paid: Rs 799 (iOS) and Rs 750 (Android) one-time payment

DSLR-level control, right from your phone

Built for photographers who like to tinker

Privacy that doesn't get compromised

What else it packs in

Should you download it

What if your phone’s camera app stopped acting like a point-and-shoot and started behaving like an actual DSLR without any computational photography ‘magic’. That’s exactly the idea behind ProShot, a manual camera app that’s already won over thousands of photographers. Instead of relying on the phone's default auto mode to make every decision for you, ProShot hands over full manual control, letting you shoot RAW images. It also allows you to fine-tune everything from exposure to white balance, just like you would on a proper camera.With ProShot, you can shoot in full manual, semi-auto, or let smart Auto handle things when you're in a hurry. Whichever mode you pick, you get direct control over exposure, ISO, white balance, and more, the same dials and settings a dedicated camera would offer.Where ProShot really stands out is in how much it lets you adjust on the fly. Its Dual Dial system is designed to let you jump between camera settings quickly, without digging through menus mid-shot. There's a dedicated button to start recording video instantly, a Bulb mode for capturing star trails or light painting, and support for remappable controls, histograms and focus peaking – tools that serious photographers typically look for in a proper camera app.ProShot keeps things clean as the company says that there is no data harvesting involved, which means your photos and personal information stay right where they belong, on your device.The photography side of ProShot reads like a checklist for a DSLR. You get Auto, Program, Manual, and two Custom modes, along with shutter priority, ISO priority and full manual controls, among other ‘Pro controls’. On the video side, ProShot brings the same level of control. You can shoot up to 8K video with high bitrate options, adjust frame rates anywhere from 24 FPS to a smooth 240 FPS, and use LOG and FLAT colour profiles for better dynamic range. It supports both H.264 and H.265 codecs, external microphones, real-time audio and file-size monitoring.If you’ve been wanting to shoot RAW photos or DSLR-style videos without lugging around an actual camera, ProShot is worth trying out. It's built for people who want real creative control over their shots.
Article Summary: ProShot lets you shoot in full manual, semi-auto, or let smart Auto handle things when you're in a hurry. Whichever mode you pick, you get direct control over exposure, ISO, white balance, and more. Its Dual Dial system is designed to let you jump between camera settings quickly, without digging through menus mid- shot.

Article Title: In 2021, a former Buddhist monk who was a software engineer at Meta 'accidentally' founded a startup that now competes with Accenture
Article Text:
Image credit: LinkedIn

Lilly Chen's path from Buddhist monk to software engineer

Contenda's startup journey began with a hackathon

A former Buddhist monk who later worked as a software engineer at Meta accidentally became a startup founder after a pandemic-era hackathon with childhood friends. In 2021, Lilly Chen and three friends turned a project they built for fun into FSH Technologies (formerly Contenda), which has since positioned itself to compete with Accenture in government contract bidding.In an interview with Constellary, Chen described the company’s beginnings as something she “fell into” rather than a business she had planned to build. Before becoming a founder, she spent two years as a Buddhist monk after leaving high school at 16, living for a period at a monastery in China. She later returned to the US, completed high school and studied mathematics and economics in college before teaching herself to code and working as a software engineer, including a stint at Facebook. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she took leave from Facebook and invited childhood friends to California, where they decided to build a project together.In another Business Insider interview, Chen noted that unlike Accenture, FSH Technologies takes a different approach to government consulting, focusing on end-to-end fixes for administrative systems rather than isolated software projects. The company does not use traditional billable consulting hours or a conventional sales-and-consultant structure, instead relying on hands-on builders to address processes, procurement rules, and other operational challenges.Chen said she left high school at 16 after dealing with a chronic illness and spent about two years as a monk, including two to three months at a remote monastery in China. The head monk eventually asked her whether she actually wanted to remain there, prompting Chen to reconsider her plans.She returned to the US, re-enrolled in high school and later attended college, where she studied mathematics and economics. Although she had considered pursuing a PhD in economics, financial responsibilities led her to seek employment instead.Without a computer science degree, Chen taught herself programming through online resources and coding exercises. Her first software engineering position was as a DevOps engineer at a gaming AI startup, after which she worked at Facebook building CI/CD pipelines for machine-learning engineers.Chen said the group initially had no plan to start a company. During her leave from Facebook, she and her friends began playing video games and decided to recreate the hackathon experience they had enjoyed in college.The group built a project to help Twitch streamer Ludwig with subscriber retention. After contacting him, they agreed to provide the service for $1 per subscriber for a month, during which he reached 200,000 subscribers.The project led the group to speak with investors. Chen said the founders initially had reservations about leaving their existing paths, particularly because some of them were still in college and she was concerned about maintaining her family’s financial stability. They ultimately accepted their first pre-seed funding of $1 million in March 2021.
Article Summary: Lilly Chen and three friends turned a project they built for fun into FSH Technologies. The company has since positioned itself to compete with Accenture in government contract bidding. Before becoming a founder, she spent two years as a Buddhist monk after leaving high school at 16.

Article Title: Jeff Dean, whose Google exit triggered $200 billion loss in a day for the company, has this say on Gemini innovation
Article Text:
Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, left after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop.

Jeff Dean gets emotional while talking about his 27-year tenure

Dean highlights power of small teams in modern AI era

Jeff Dean, longtime computing pioneer at Google , has spoken publicly for the first time since departing the company, expressing strong faith in the direction of the company’s Gemini artificial intelligence models while explaining his move to launch a four-person startup. Dean’s resignation sent shockwaves through Wall Street, causing Alphabet shares to tumble 3.9% and erasing nearly $190 billion in market capitalisation in a single day.Addressing an audience at Stanford University during an event on August 7 (as per Business Insider), Dean grew visibly emotional when discussing his choice to step away from the tech giant after more than 27 years. In video footage released on August 18, Dean offered a thumbs-up gesture while holding back tears.“I don't attribute things in the stock market to any particular events because it's always hard,” he said of Google losing $200 billion in a day. Alphabet reportedly closed down 3.9%, giving up roughly $190 billion of market value, after Jeff Dean and three colleagues resigned to found Discovery Loop.“You know I think first I have incredible fondness for my time at Google. I've been there for 27 years. Amazing colleagues. So they're in good shape. They have a plan for making the Gemini models awesome. It's gonna be great,” he said while talking about Gemini innovation.Dean established a landmark reputation throughout his near three-decade run at Google by heading several of the firm's most critical technical initiatives.During the discussion, Dean highlighted why smaller organisations are now uniquely positioned to drive rapid breakthroughs. Rather than needing massive corporate machinery, Dean pointed out that early-stage teams have a common focus.“I'm excited to go off and do this. I think it's going to be really, really fun. Sometimes a focused small company with everyone focused on exactly that mission. And I think it's a great mission. It’s going to be amazing,” he noted.Dean quit Google to build his own AI startup called Discovery Loop which is backed by Google.
Article Summary: Jeff Dean, Google's 30th employee and chief scientist, left after 27 years to lead AI startup Discovery Loop. Dean's resignation sent shockwaves through Wall Street, causing Alphabet shares to tumble 3.9% and erasing nearly $190 billion in market capitalisation in a single day.
